question: EU digital policy places emphasis on European control over data and reducing dependence on non-EU cloud infrastructure. In particular, the Data Act and the EU’s emerging cloud sovereignty framework reflect growing policy emphasis on the protection and, where appropriate, storage and processing of data within the EU.

However, widely used business software, largely supplied by non-EU cloud vendors, often makes storage in the EU a premium feature. Several vendors operate data centres in the EU but restrict their use to enterprise tiers at unpublished prices. On the standard plans which small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can afford, data is stored outside the EU with no options offered.

Comparable vendors offer region selection in standard tiers, indicating that this is a commercial choice. For SMEs, storing data in Europe has become a luxury – a sovereignty premium set against expectations EU policy itself creates. 1.
Has the Commission assessed the practice of restricting data-residency options within the EU to premium pricing tiers, and its impact on SMEs?
Does the Commission consider this practice compatible with the Data Act and the EU’s cloud sovereignty agenda?

Will the Commission consider requiring that providers operating EU data centres offer region-of-storage choice on standard commercial terms, or at minimum per-tier transparency on where data is stored?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.11.2026) Businesses should have clear information and control about where their data is stored. This is important for businesses of all sizes, including small and medium-sized enterprises (‘SMEs’), and to achieve digital sovereignty objectives.

Available market information does not currently provide sufficient evidence to conclude that EU data residency is not generally available for SMEs. The Data Act1 facilitates switching between cloud providers to reduce customer lock-in and to promote an open and competitive cloud market in the EU.

It also provides legal protection for non-personal data hosted by data processing services in the EU, making foreign governmental data access requests subject to the presence of mutual legal assistance treaties or to guarantees of rule of law and judicial appeal. The proposal for a Cloud and AI Development Act2 aims to strengthen Europe’s cloud and AI capabilities.

It establishes a sovereignty framework for the public procurement of cloud computing services. It will help scale sovereign cloud services, also benefitting SMEs. The Commission continues to monitor developments in the cloud sector and to support the development of competitive, secure and reliable cloud services in Europe.
In this context, the availability and accessibility of cloud services for businesses of all sizes, including SMEs, remain important considerations.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2023 on

harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data and amending Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2854/oj). 2 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a framework of measures for strengthening Europe’s cloud and AI ecosystem (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026PC0502).
